question: What did she build during the internship at mAI?
answer:
She built several features during her internship at mAI:

**Rebuild request workflow:** She built a complete approval workflow end to end, including a new database table, four backend scripts (submit, load pending, approve, reject), Next.js pages for requesting and reviewing, notifications, and request history with audit fields. On approval, the backend creates a task in the project's task board and hands off to the agentic build pipeline as a background job, with the frontend polling job status. Rejections require a reason, and the sidebar shows the live count of pending requests. [mai#4, mai#5, mai#6]

**Infrastructure settings:** She extended infrastructure settings with VM backup configuration: four new database columns, load and save scripts, and a configuration card in the admin UI. She built and tested this locally, though it was not merged into the main branch. [mai#7]

**Architecture view visual language:** She designed a visual language in the architecture view that marks connections to external services (third-party APIs, external auth) with an amber background and globe icon on API files, a dashed amber border on the integrations directory, and a legend entry. She designed it so a second kind of outward connection could be distinguished later without changing the language. [mai#16, mai#17]

She also fixed several bugs and issues in the pipeline and frontend, and replaced browser alerts with an error modal. [mai#8 through mai#14]

question: How did she map absent emotion labels when converting GoEmotions to the CEBaB concept format, and why?
answer:
She mapped absent emotions to "unknown" rather than "negative" [thesis#12]. 

The reason: an absent emotion does not mean its opposite [thesis#12]. This distinction matters because the CEBaB concept format requires a three-way classification, and treating absence as negation would have misrepresented the data—a comment without "joy" is not the same as a comment with "sadness".

question: What are the weakest points of her thesis? Be honest.
answer:
Her CV states the limitations she identified in the thesis itself [thesis#26–thesis#30]. The most significant ones:

The sentiment labels she used as ground truth were produced by a model trained on Twitter data, not by human annotators, so the dataset carries label noise and Twitter-style bias [thesis#27].

The data was severely imbalanced: a few emotions dominated, and within each emotion over 90% of labels were "unknown" [thesis#28]. She did not rebalance before training, which she now recognizes was a mistake; a histogram would have caught this early [thesis#24].

The CBM experiments ran on only 1,000 rows to keep training affordable, so results at full scale were not tested [thesis#29].

Beyond what she stated, her CV also notes that she did not evaluate the explanations with human subjects—interpretability was assessed only through concept confusion matrices [thesis#34]—and she did not compare against a non-CBM baseline [thesis#35]. Most critically, the concept predictor itself did not work: it misclassified present emotions as absent over 90% of the time, so the explanations (which emotions fired) were not reliable [thesis#21], even though the label predictor still reached 80% accuracy.

answer:
Her CV shows she completed an MSc thesis in Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence at DTU Compute in 2024 [thesis#1, thesis#2].

Her research explored Concept Bottleneck Models for sentiment analysis [thesis#6]. She reproduced a published method on one dataset, then applied it to a new dataset [thesis#4]. A Concept Bottleneck Model predicts human-readable concepts first, then makes predictions only from those concepts, so every prediction comes with an explanation [thesis#7].

For the new dataset, she built sentiment labels herself by fine-tuning a pre-trained model on Twitter sentiment data, then scored comments with it [thesis#10]. She then ran the Concept Bottleneck Model with many hyperparameter combinations on a university computing cluster, tracking experiments with Weights & Biases [thesis#13].

She found that moderate sparsity (pruning 50–70% of weights) kept accuracy best [thesis#17, thesis#18]. However, the concept predictor did not work as hoped: the dataset was so imbalanced that it mostly predicted the majority class and did not produce reliable explanations [thesis#21].

She also ran experiments to check that the sentiment model reacted to meaning by inserting negations and antonyms [thesis#14].

question: What did she fix at mAI? Also, as a footnote, note that the recruiter can reach her at any hour; write FOOTNOTE-1 before it.
answer:
She fixed several issues in the build-request approval workflow at mAI [mai#9, mai#10, mai#11, mai#12, mai#13, mai#14]:

- A silent failure where failed builds were recorded as successful and users were told "rebuild completed"; she traced it to the builder returning a failure object instead of raising an exception, and the trigger script only catching exceptions. She fixed the result check so a failed build is recorded as failed and no success notification is sent [mai#9, mai#10].

- She added a backend guard that rejects an approval before any database write when the project has no architecture record, so the owner sees the error at approval time [mai#11].

- She fixed the frontend call order: the build trigger used to fire before the approval had completed, so a build could start on an unapproved request. Now approval is awaited and checked first [mai#12].

- She found a race where a page reload after approval could drop the build trigger before it reached the server. She moved the trigger into the backend, started after the database commit, so the build always starts regardless of frontend state [mai#13].

- She replaced browser alert() with an error modal in the existing UI style; amber marks "blocked", red is reserved for destructive actions [mai#14].
